summary:
Putrajaya, a federal territory of Malaysia, stands under the national framework: Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at federal level, while the territory's own Sharia code adds a second layer that reaches Muslims only.

Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. The provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Sharia enactments in all 13 states and in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only, they are enforced by state Islamic religious departments, and they contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia. There is no same-sex marriage and no general anti-discrimination law.

Courts have narrowed the Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court refused to declare the cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge had been pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement is raid-based and public rather than directed at individuals. Since the 2018 election police have detained at least 20 LGBT people at a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur in October 2022 and twenty men at an LGBT venue in August 2022. On 28 November 2025 they arrested 208 men under section 377B at a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, the largest operation of its kind since 2022; media had been pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet more than 130 people were held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Official policy targets gender nonconformity directly. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Trans women in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself". A Terengganu Sharia court has ordered a lesbian couple caned.

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, Johor planned conversion-therapy centres in November 2023, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters published "I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia" on 10 August 2022, drawing on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia conducted between 2018 and 2021. The report places conversion and "rehabilitation" practices alongside criminal penalties as the main instruments of state pressure.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Malaysia was last updated on 16 December 2025 and records discrimination and violence against LGBT people as regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. Its enforcement examples postdate the 2018 election, which is the relevant period for judging current practice rather than inherited statute.

The cross-dressing regime is national in shape, not peculiar to Putrajaya: all 13 states have passed such enactments since the 1980s and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Sub-national litigation has produced relief in only two instances, both on federalism grounds rather than on rights grounds.

Raids carry reputational consequences beyond detention. After the November 2025 Chow Kit operation, 17 civil servants identified among the detainees were suspended, and Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid for those held. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, a sign of official awareness of the operation's cost.
localsOnly:
Malaysian residents who are Muslim face two overlapping regimes: the federal Penal Code and their state's Sharia enactment against cross-dressing, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Enforcement sits with state Islamic religious departments, which in the Federal Territories acted under an explicit ministerial mandate issued in July 2020.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, no statutory protection against discrimination, and no access to same-sex marriage. LGBT events and media content are censored, and government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021.

Police treatment of detained trans people is documented as abusive and impunity as routine, as in the Klang killing of 25 June 2019. Residents arrested in the November 2025 Chow Kit raid faced public exposure of their identities; 17 of them were civil servants and were suspended.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement case specific to Putrajaya itself is documented in the sources reviewed; the raid evidence comes from Kuala Lumpur, Penang, Johor, Terengganu and Selangor, and the national framework is what governs a visitor's exposure here. That gap is unresolved rather than evidence of non-enforcement.

The sources do not state whether Putrajaya's own Sharia enactment differs in wording or penalties from the other states' cross-dressing provisions beyond the shared elements listed above. Whether any administrative or court-based gender-recognition route exists despite the absence of a recorded statutory procedure is likewise unsourced.

No figure is available for visitors or non-Muslims prosecuted under sections 377A and 377B, nor for the outcome of the charges arising from the 28 November 2025 operation, including whether the foreign nationals held were deported, charged or released. Detention conditions and placement of trans detainees are not covered by these sources.
